items.item: The table in examples.py is real -- a real pyiceberg table whose partition spec is evolved with the real table.update_spec() API (remove_field/add_field), not a simulation of spec evolution -- with every structural and pruning claim read directly off table.specs(), table.inspect.data_files(), table.inspect.manifests(), and table.scan(...).plan_files(), disclosed in the script's own docstring and FACT-CHECK.md red-team #1.
Old-data-not-rewritten is checked positively, not merely not disproven: data_files() is filtered by the old spec's id and the surviving file count is asserted, per FACT-CHECK.md red-team #2.

at.step: Reveal: reproduced for real — the old era’s files stay on disk under the old spec

items.item: The each-manifest-planned-under-its-own-spec claim is measured, not inferred: the two files returned for the old-era and new-era queries are asserted to have different spec_id values, proof planning consulted each file's own recorded spec, per FACT-CHECK.md red-team #3.

at.step: Reveal: reproduced for real — a source-column query prunes to one file in either era

items.item: v3 multi-argument transforms are named from the spec's own v3 writing rules, not built, since this sandbox's pyiceberg table defaults to format version 2, per FACT-CHECK.md red-team #4.
identity and truncate[W] are named from the spec but not executed in examples.py, which builds only day, hour, and bucket[N] -- named as a scope boundary in FACT-CHECK.md red-team #5.
File paths and UUIDs are real-system randomness; the script asserts and prints counts and structure, not literal paths, verified byte-identical across 3 consecutive runs.
